title: Where things are
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: ONE PREPOSITION, TWO CASES, TWO MEANINGS. in with the -ā shape is 'in / on' and says where you ARE: in scholā sum. in with the -am shape is 'into' and says where you are GOING: in scholam eō. English has one 'in' for both and lets the verb sort it out; Latin puts the difference on the noun, and getting it wrong changes the sentence.

This is the module where English prepositions become case endings. The -ā on scholā and the -ē on mēnsā are doing what 'in' and 'on' do in English — so a Latin place-phrase is a preposition AND an ending, and dropping the ending leaves the preposition with nothing to govern.

Every preposition governs one case, and which one is part of the word. ad, apud and prope take the object shape; cum takes the -ā shape. Only in takes both, and only in changes meaning when it does. Learn each preposition with its case, the way you learn a verb with its family.

hic and hīc are two different words, one bar apart. hic is 'this' and hīc is 'here' — and both are useful in exactly this module, so they are taught together rather than one at a time. Say hīc long and hic short, and a Roman will hear which you meant.

'This' bends for the gender of what it points at: hic liber (a book), haec mēnsa (a table), hoc nōmen (a name). Three shapes for one English word, and the ending follows the noun rather than the speaker.

est does 'there is' with no extra machinery: In mēnsā est liber, 'on the table there is a book'. English needs a dummy 'there'; Latin needs word order, and what it wants is the thing being located LAST.

Place names work differently and this course has not taught them yet. 'In Rome' is not in Rōmā but Rōmae, a surviving shape with only a handful of members — it is deferred to a later level, so use in with an ordinary noun here.

words.note: 'In / on' with the -ā shape (where you are), 'into' with the -am shape (where you are going). One word, two cases, two meanings.

words.cue: school (as the place you are in)
words.note: The -ā shape of M4's schola, used after in for being somewhere and after cum for being with something. The bar is the whole ending.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: The long ā is the word 'at'. Write schola and the sentence says something else; write scholam and it says you are going in. English puts the whole meaning in the preposition and Latin splits it between the preposition and the ending.
sentences.sound: IN SCHO-lā SUM. Hold the ā — it is the only thing separating this from 'into school'.

variations.changed: the verb ending moves it to 'you'
and to a third person
a different place, and the same -ā shape doing 'on' instead of 'in'

mistake.why: The 'into' shape used for being somewhere. With sum the sentence cannot mean motion, so a Roman would hear a contradiction — the noun says you are going and the verb says you are standing still.

sentences.usage: Said about where you are now.
sentences.mnemonic: Long ā, standing still. Short -am, moving in.

words.note: 'In / on' with the -ā shape (where you are), 'into' with the -am shape (where you are going). One word, two cases, two meanings.
'School' — schola as the subject, scholam after ad and after in when in means 'into'. In Latin it meant the teaching rather than the building.
'I go': eō, īs 'you go', it 'he/she goes', īre 'to go'. Tiny and irregular — it is a complete sentence on its own.

sentences.trap: Compare M4's ad scholam eō: ad is 'to' and in with this shape is 'into'. Both take the same ending, and the difference between arriving at a place and entering it is carried by the preposition alone.
sentences.sound: IN SCHO-lam E-ō. Clip the -am; it is short, and that shortness is the case.

variations.changed: a third person; the case does not move
a different preposition over the same ending, and a slightly different arrival

variations.cue: I want to go into school.
variations.changed: M3's wanting over the top, with the infinitive first

mistake.why: The 'where you are' shape with a verb of motion. It is the exact mirror of S01's mistake: the noun says you are standing still and the verb says you are moving.

words.note: 'Where', and it goes first, as in English. It asks about being somewhere rather than about going — so its answer is an -ā shape, never an -am one.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.
'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one. Here it is what the question is about, so it is the plain shape.

sentences.trap: No -ne is needed. A question with a question word in it does not take the particle M2 taught — ubi already makes it a question, and adding -ne would be asking twice.
sentences.sound: U-bi est LI-ber. Three short words; nothing in the line is held.

variations.changed: a different thing asked about
the person asked about, with no noun at all
a person as the thing located

mistake.why: The question particle added to a question word. -ne turns a STATEMENT into a yes/no question; ubi already asks for a place, so the two do different jobs and never stack.

sentences.usage: Said when you have lost something.
sentences.mnemonic: ubi asks; -ne asks a different kind of question.

sentences.cue: The book is on the table.

words.note: 'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one. Here it is what is being located, so it is the plain shape.
'In / on' with the -ā shape (where you are), 'into' with the -am shape (where you are going). One word, two cases, two meanings.

words.cue: table (as the place something is on)
words.note: 'Table': mēnsa as the subject, mēnsam as the object, mēnsā after in or cum. The ē is long in all three.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: One Latin word covers 'in' and 'on'. Latin does not care whether you are inside a thing or resting on it — in plus the -ā shape does both, and the noun tells you which is meant.
sentences.sound: LI-ber in MEN-sā est. Two long vowels in mēnsā, one after the other, and the stress on the first.

variations.cue: There is a book on the table.
variations.changed: the thing located moved to the end, which turns it into 'there is'

variations.cue: The water is on the table.
variations.changed: a different thing located

variations.cue: The books are on the table.
variations.changed: more than one, so the verb becomes sunt

mistake.why: The 'into' shape where nothing is moving. It would mean the book is in the act of going into the table, which is not a thing — and est is the clue that the -ā shape was wanted.

sentences.usage: Said in answer to ubi est.
sentences.mnemonic: in plus long ā: in it, on it, at it.

words.note: 'Here', with a LONG i. Its short twin hic means 'this' — one bar apart, and both are in this module so the pair can be learned together.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.
'Water': aqua as the subject, aquam as the object, aquā after in, cum or opus est. Three shapes of one word.

sentences.trap: hīc with the bar is 'here'. Without it you have written 'this', which is S07's word — and the two sentences differ by that one mark and by nothing else.
sentences.sound: HEEK est A-qua. Hold the ī and say the c as a k. Then say S07's hic short and quick, and the pair separates cleanly.

variations.changed: a different thing located
the person located, with no noun
the opposite word — here becomes there and nothing else moves

mistake.why: The bar dropped, which turns 'here' into 'this'. The sentence now says 'this is water', which is a real sentence and a different one — and nothing but the macron distinguishes them.

sentences.usage: Said when pointing at where something is.
sentences.mnemonic: Long ī, a place. Short i, a thing.

words.note: 'There', the opposite of hīc — and unlike hīc it has no near twin, so nothing about it can be misread. Both vowels are short.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.
'School' — schola as the subject, scholam after ad, scholā after in. In Latin it meant the teaching rather than the building.

sentences.trap: schola is the plain shape here because it is the subject, not a place. Being a word about a place does not make a noun take a place ending — the job in the sentence decides, and here its job is to be what the sentence is about.
sentences.sound: I-bi est SCHO-la. Nothing long anywhere; the whole line is light.

variations.changed: a different thing located
the person located
the order reversed, which puts the weight on the school

mistake.why: A place ending put on the subject because the sentence is about a place. scholā is what you use after in; as the thing being talked about, the school takes its plain shape.

words.note: 'This', bending for what it points at: hic liber, haec mēnsa, hoc nōmen. Its i is SHORT — the long hīc is 'here'.
'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one. Here it is what the sentence is about.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: Hic liber est reads both 'this is a book' and 'this book is…', and only the situation tells you which. Latin is content with that ambiguity; English is not, which is why the sentence feels unfinished.
sentences.sound: HIC LI-ber est. Short i — clipped. Beside S05's HEEK the difference is the whole of the two words.

variations.changed: a feminine noun, so 'this' becomes haec
a neuter noun, so 'this' becomes hoc — three genders, three shapes
a person pointed at, with the same masculine shape

mistake.why: The masculine 'this' with a feminine noun. hic follows the gender of what it points at, so a table takes haec — and the two words have to agree even though only one of them carries the meaning 'this'.

sentences.usage: Said when you are pointing at something close by.
sentences.mnemonic: hic, haec, hoc — three genders of one small word.

words.note: 'At the house of, in the presence of', and it takes the object shape. It is used of PEOPLE rather than places — apud magistrum, not apud scholam.

words.cue: teacher (as the person you are at)
words.note: The object shape of M1's magister, used after ad, apud and prope. The e drops out whenever an ending is added.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: apud takes the object shape even though nothing is moving. The case a preposition governs has nothing to do with motion — only in changes its case for that reason, and every other preposition has one case and keeps it.
sentences.sound: A-pud ma-GIS-trum SUM. The d at the end of apud is said, lightly.

variations.changed: a third person; the case does not move
the verb ending moves it to you; the case does not move
a different preposition, and it governs the same case

mistake.why: The -ā-type shape used because the sentence is about being somewhere. apud governs the object shape and always does — the meaning of the sentence does not get a vote.

sentences.usage: Said about being at someone's house or in their company.
sentences.mnemonic: apud is for people, in is for places.

words.note: 'Near', and it takes the object shape like ad and apud. English 'approach' and 'propinquity' both keep it.

words.cue: table (as the thing you are near)
words.note: 'Table': mēnsa as the subject, mēnsam as the object, mēnsā after in or cum. The ē is long in all three.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: Three prepositions now take the object shape — ad, apud, prope — and one takes the -ā shape. The pattern is not 'motion takes the object': it is that each word carries its own case, and you learn them as pairs.
sentences.sound: PRO-pe MEN-sam SUM. The final e of prope is short and said; it is not silent as in English 'rope'.

variations.changed: a third person
a different thing to be near

variations.cue: The book is near the table.
variations.changed: a thing located rather than a person

mistake.why: The wrong case again, and for the same reason: 'near the table' feels like a place and places feel like they want the -ā shape. prope does not care — it governs the object shape.

sentences.usage: Said about being close to something.
sentences.mnemonic: ad, apud, prope: all three take the -m.

words.note: 'With', and it takes the -ā-type shape rather than the object one. A later level uses this same spelling as 'when'; here it is only ever 'with'.

words.cue: teacher (as the person you are with)
words.note: The -ō shape of M1's magister, used after cum and in. Nouns like magister take -ō where nouns like schola take -ā.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: The ending after cum is -ō here and -ā after schola. It is the same case in both, and which letter it uses depends on the noun's family — exactly as the object shape was -am for aqua and -em for pānis in M3.
sentences.sound: CUM ma-GIS-trō SUM. The long ō at the end of magistrō is the case; hold it.

variations.changed: a third person
a name, taking the same -ō shape

variations.cue: I am at school with the teacher.
variations.changed: two place-phrases in one sentence, each with its own preposition and ending

mistake.why: The object shape after cum, which governs the other case. Three of this module's prepositions take the object shape and cum does not — it is the one to memorise as an exception.

sentences.usage: Said about whose company you are in.
sentences.mnemonic: cum takes the long ending: cum magistrō, cum mēnsā.

comprehensionPool.cue: There are books on the table.
The book is there, not here.
I will go into school tomorrow.
There is a table near the school.
I am at school with the teacher.
Where is the water? It is here.
